source.title_on_document: Introducing AI to an Online Petition Platform Changed Outputs but not Outcomes

supplement.where: SI Appendix, pp. 21-78 of this PDF; petition metadata and code on OSF (https://osf.io/q3hj5/?view_only=3fc5b89d05eb4741957af431b107cf2a), pp. 14-15, Data Availability and Code Availability. Full petition text and user names are not posted; published academic researchers can request the full text from the authors.
supplement.holds: Static DiD tables with SEs and CIs (Tables 9-19, pp. 60-62; Table 14 = mean pairwise similarity), labeling-task details and t-tests (pp. 67-68), robustness and synthetic-control figures, repeat-writer model tables (Tables 20-21)

paper_design_summary: Natural experiment on Change.org: an in-platform 'write with AI' drafting tool (built on an OpenAI-provided LLM) launched fully in the US, Great Britain, and Canada in October 2023 and only in late December 2023 in Australia. The authors run static and dynamic difference-in-differences on country-week series of English petitions (65 pre-AI weeks, 11 post-AI weeks; Australia as control) for lexical features (MATTR, Flesch-Kincaid grade, word count), homogeneity (mean pairwise cosine similarity of text-embedding-3-large embeddings within country-week), and engagement thresholds (1+ comment in 30 days, preregistered primary; 10+ signatures). Two side analyses: 14 graduate-student raters scored writing quality and persuasiveness of 417 sampled pre-AI and post-AI petitions, and a mixed-model comparison of first and second petitions by 4,611 repeat writers in treated countries.

assignment.what_was_assigned: No researcher assignment of people. In-platform AI access followed a country rollout: full access in the United States, Great Britain and Canada in October 2023, with Australia delayed until late December 2023. Country-week series are compared before and after the rollout, excluding the A/B testing period (PDF pp. 3, 12-13 and 65).
assignment.quote: The delay was due to internal logistics, and was not an intentional experiment (as far as the authors are aware).
assignment.locator: PDF pp. 12-13, Difference-in-Differences Design; p. 65, SI Change.org and the Write with AI Tool. Unit denotes country rollout; structure combines between-country and within-country time comparisons.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 3 and p. 66, SI Preregistration: https://aspredicted.org/xtcd-tvqk.pdf. Reported deviations: English threshold increased from 25% to 50%; petitions with fewer than 5 words or 2 sentences excluded; main analysis did not use inverse propensity weighting. Homogeneity was added to the preregistered analysis (p. 5).

arms.name: Treated countries (United States, Great Britain, Canada)
arms.description: Country-week series before and after full rollout; in-platform AI available during October 2-December 15, 2023, but not in the pre-AI baseline. Actual use is not assigned. Writer count is not stated (PDF pp. 2-3, 12-13).

arms.name: Australia (delayed-access control)
arms.description: Country-week series over the same periods, without in-platform AI during the main differential-access period; rollout in late December 2023. Writer count is not stated (PDF pp. 12-13 and 65).

participants.exclusions: Main subset restricted to English-language petitions in the four study countries and main date window, with at least 2 sentences and 5 words (PDF p. 11). English requires the page language tag and at least 50% of words recognized as English; the A/B period is excluded from the main DiD (PDF pp. 3 and 65). These are petition filters; no number of excluded people is reported.
participants.who: Corpus of Change.org petitions: 1,517,433 petitions posted 2022-2024; main causal subset N = 361,635 English petitions from the US, Canada, Great Britain, and Australia posted January 3, 2022 to December 15, 2023 with at least 2 sentences and 5 words; static DiD uses 279,131 petitions (65 pre-AI weeks, N = 237,020; 11 post-AI weeks, N = 42,111; A/B test period excluded), aggregated to 304 country-week observations. Number of writers not stated for this analysis.
participants.country: United States, Great Britain, Canada (treated); Australia (control)
participants.quote: The main causal analysis of our study uses a subset (N = 361,635) of petitions that are English language, posted by users in the United States, Canada, Great Britain, and Australia
participants.locator: PDF p. 11, Materials and Methods, Data; p. 13 (279,131 petitions); p. 61, SI Table 14 (304 observations); p. 65, SI Data (filters and period counts)

ai_tool.name_model: Change.org in-platform 'write with AI' tool built on an OpenAI-provided LLM (model not named)
ai_tool.how_used: Generates a full petition draft from a short user-entered description of a cause; treatment is access to the tool, not measured use (the authors' classifier flags over half of post-access petitions as AI-generated, SI Fig. 2)

task.description: Writing and posting real advocacy petitions on Change.org

outcomes.name: Platform homogeneity: mean pairwise cosine similarity of petition embeddings within a country-week (higher similarity means lower diversity)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Petition embeddings are compared across all pairs within each country-week and averaged into one score (PDF p. 5, Platform Homogeneity). This analysis was added to the preregistered analysis. Static and dynamic DiD are variants of this outcome; the static model has 304 country-week observations (PDF p. 61, SI Table 14). Coefficients retain the original similarity sign.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Treated countries (US, GB, CA), post-AI weeks (Oct 2 - Dec 15, 2023)
contrasts.control_arm: Australia and pre-AI weeks (static DiD, country and week fixed effects, SEs clustered by month)
contrasts.reported: Static DiD, Treated Country x Post-AI: estimate 0.056, Std. Error 0.003, CIs [0.049, 0.063], t 17.825, p 0.000, Observations 304 (Table 14). Main text: 0.056 (95% CI = [0.049, 0.063], t(17) = 17.83, p < 0.001), 'a 23% increase from the average pre-AI weekly mean similarity value of 0.240'. Dynamic DiD: about 0.05 units per post-AI week (Fig. 2).
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Platform Homogeneity and Figure 2; p. 61, SI Table 14

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of petition embeddings; higher similarity means greater homogeneity and lower diversity (PDF p. 5, Platform Homogeneity).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, 3,072 dimensions (PDF p. 5, Platform Homogeneity).
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of petitions posted in a given week and country; pairwise scores are averaged into one country-week score. Static model: 304 observations; 65 pre-AI weeks and 11 post-AI weeks, excluding the A/B period (PDF pp. 5 and 13; p. 61, SI Table 14).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Static DiD is described as OLS with country and week fixed effects, using the R did package to estimate ATT weighted by group size; standard errors clustered by month, with a t-distribution with 17 degrees of freedom (PDF p. 13; p. 61, SI Table 14). Dynamic DiD uses a multiplier bootstrap with 1,000 iterations and simultaneous 95% confidence bands (PDF p. 5, Figure 2; p. 69, SI Difference-in-Differences).
diversity_detail.notes: Added to the preregistered analysis (PDF p. 5). The positive coefficient is an increase in similarity and has not been numerically reversed. Pairs are defined over petitions; distinct writer counts are not stated. No separate homogeneity robustness specification is reported in the SI.

outcomes.name: Share of petitions with 1+ comment in 30 days (preregistered primary engagement outcome)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Weekly country-level percentage of petitions receiving at least one comment from someone other than the author within 30 days of posting (PDF pp. 5 and 12). Production occurs with AI available in the treatment period; engagement is subsequently observed. Country-clustered robustness: estimate -2.508 percentage points, SE 1.822, 95% CI [-8.308, 3.291], t -1.376, p 0.262, 304 observations (PDF p. 61, SI Table 15). Other variants are alternative engagement thresholds and log counts (PDF p. 33, SI Figure 11), a 25-week pre-period (pp. 35 and 69, Figure 13), all of December (pp. 36 and 70, Figure 14), short petitions included (pp. 37 and 70, Figure 15), topic subsets (pp. 40 and 49-50, Figures 19 and 30-31), excluding the US (p. 45, Figure 25), individual-country comparisons (p. 46, Figure 26), and synthetic controls (pp. 53-55 and 75, Figures 34-36). The doubly robust covariate analysis shows no directional difference in outcomes (pp. 38 and 70, Figure 16). An interrupted-time-series variant uses the start of A/B testing (pp. 58 and 76, Figure 39).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Treated countries (US, GB, CA), post-AI weeks
contrasts.reported: Static DiD, Treated Country x Post-AI: estimate -2.508 (percentage points), Std. Error 1.826, CIs [-6.360, 1.343], t -1.374, p 0.187, Observations 304 (Table 9). Main text: -2.51 percentage points (95% CI = [-6.36, 1.34], t(17) = -1.37, p = 0.187).
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Outcomes; p. 4, Figure 1d; p. 60, SI Table 9

outcomes.name: Share of petitions with 10+ signatures
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Weekly country-level percentage of petitions reaching at least 10 signatures at data collection; signature dates are unavailable, so this is not a 30-day signature endpoint (PDF pp. 5 and 12). Country-clustered robustness: estimate -5.329 percentage points, SE 1.973, 95% CI [-11.609, 0.950], t -2.701, p 0.074, 304 observations (PDF p. 61, SI Table 16); unlike the month-clustered main estimate, this interval includes zero. Other variants are alternative engagement thresholds and log counts (PDF p. 33, SI Figure 11), a 25-week pre-period (pp. 35 and 69, Figure 13), all of December (pp. 36 and 70, Figure 14), short petitions included (pp. 37 and 70, Figure 15), topic subsets (pp. 40 and 49-50, Figures 19 and 30-31), excluding the US (p. 45, Figure 25), individual-country comparisons (p. 46, Figure 26), and synthetic controls (pp. 53-55 and 75, Figures 34-36). The doubly robust covariate analysis shows no directional difference in outcomes (pp. 38 and 70, Figure 16). An interrupted-time-series variant uses the start of A/B testing (pp. 58 and 76, Figure 39).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Treated countries (US, GB, CA), post-AI weeks
contrasts.reported: Static DiD, Treated Country x Post-AI: estimate -5.329 (percentage points), Std. Error 1.363, CIs [-8.205, -2.454], t -3.911, p 0.001, Observations 304 (Table 10). Main text: -5.33 percentage points (95% CI = [-8.21, -2.45], t(17) = -3.91, p = .001).
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Outcomes; p. 4, Figure 1d; p. 60, SI Table 10

outcomes.name: Petition length: weekly median word count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of space-separated tokens in the title and body, aggregated to the country-week median (PDF pp. 11-13). Static and dynamic DiD are variants. Country-clustered robustness: estimate 53.628, SE 4.584, 95% CI [39.040, 68.215], t 11.699, p 0.001, 304 observations (PDF p. 62, SI Table 18). Sentence count is an additional length measure with a significant increase (pp. 34 and 69, SI Figure 12). The government-topic subset has no significant increase in word count (pp. 40 and 70-71, SI Figure 19). Other robustness variants include a shorter pre-period, all of December, short petitions included, covariate adjustment, topic subsets, excluding the US, individual-country comparisons and synthetic controls (PDF pp. 35-40, 45-46, 49-55, 69-70 and 75). An interrupted-time-series analysis uses the start of A/B testing (pp. 58 and 76, SI Figure 39).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Treated countries (US, GB, CA), post-AI weeks
contrasts.control_arm: Australia and pre-AI weeks (static DiD; country and week fixed effects; month-clustered SEs)
contrasts.reported: Static DiD, Treated Country x Post-AI: estimate 53.628 words, Std. Error 3.105, 95% CIs [47.077, 60.178], t 17.273, p 0.000, Observations 304 (Table 12). Main text: 53.63 words (95% CI [47.08, 60.18], t(17) = 17.27, p < 0.001), a 49% increase from 110 words pre-AI.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, Lexical Features and Figure 1; p. 61, SI Table 12

outcomes.name: Within-petition lexical diversity: weekly median MATTR
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Moving average type-token ratio over 50-word windows in title and body, then the country-week median (PDF pp. 11-13). This measures vocabulary variation within a petition, not diversity across writers. Static and dynamic DiD are variants. Country-clustered robustness: estimate 0.049, SE 0.002, 95% CI [0.042, 0.055], t 23.150, p 0.000, 304 observations (PDF p. 62, SI Table 17). Other robustness variants include a shorter pre-period, all of December, short petitions included, covariate adjustment, topic subsets, excluding the US, individual-country comparisons and synthetic controls (PDF pp. 35-40, 45-46, 49-55, 69-70 and 75). An interrupted-time-series analysis uses the start of A/B testing (pp. 58 and 76, SI Figure 39).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Treated countries (US, GB, CA), post-AI weeks
contrasts.control_arm: Australia and pre-AI weeks (static DiD; country and week fixed effects; month-clustered SEs)
contrasts.reported: Static DiD, Treated Country x Post-AI: estimate 0.049, Std. Error 0.001, 95% CIs [0.047, 0.050], t 61.482, p 0.000, Observations 304 (Table 11). Main text: 0.049 (95% CI [0.047, 0.050], t(17) = 61.48, p < 0.001), a 6% increase from 0.8 pre-AI.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, Lexical Features and Figure 1; p. 60, SI Table 11

outcomes.name: Text complexity: weekly median Flesch-Kincaid grade level
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Flesch-Kincaid grade level on title and body, using words per sentence and syllables per word, aggregated to the country-week median. Higher scores mean more complex text (PDF pp. 3 and 11-13). Static and dynamic DiD are variants. Country-clustered robustness: estimate 1.487, SE 0.064, 95% CI [1.284, 1.690], t 23.299, p 0.000, 304 observations (PDF p. 62, SI Table 19). Alternative complexity/readability measures (words per sentence, characters per word, Gunning Fog index) also increase (pp. 34 and 69, SI Figure 12). Other robustness variants include a shorter pre-period, all of December, short petitions included, covariate adjustment, topic subsets, excluding the US, individual-country comparisons and synthetic controls (PDF pp. 35-40, 45-46, 49-55, 69-70 and 75). An interrupted-time-series analysis uses the start of A/B testing (pp. 58 and 76, SI Figure 39).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Treated countries (US, GB, CA), post-AI weeks
contrasts.control_arm: Australia and pre-AI weeks (static DiD; country and week fixed effects; month-clustered SEs)
contrasts.reported: Static DiD, Treated Country x Post-AI: estimate 1.487 grades, Std. Error 0.162, 95% CIs [1.144, 1.830], t 9.157, p 0.000, Observations 304 (Table 13). Main text: 1.49 grades (95% CI [1.14, 1.83], t(17) = 9.16, p < 0.001), a 19% increase from grade 8 pre-AI.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 4, Lexical Features and Figure 1; p. 61, SI Table 13

studies.label: Petition writing quality and persuasiveness labeling task (pre-AI vs post-AI sample)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Petitions were sampled from pre-AI and post-AI periods. Raters received random sets of existing petitions; petition writers were not assigned to AI access or use (PDF p. 67).
assignment.quote: We randomly sampled 432 English language petitions from our dataset, such that 216 were from the pre-AI period and 216 were from the post-AI period.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 67, SI Petition Writing Quality and Persuasiveness. Unit denotes sampled petitions, not random assignment of people to AI.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 66, SI Preregistration: https://aspredicted.org/z6g8xe.pdf; authors report no deviations for the labeling task. No primary labeling outcome is identified in the paper.

arms.name: Post-AI petitions
arms.description: 214 petitions analyzed, sampled from the period with in-platform AI access; unique writer count not reported. This is an output count (PDF p. 67).

arms.name: Pre-AI petitions
arms.description: 203 petitions analyzed, sampled before in-platform AI access; unique writer count not reported. This is an output count (PDF p. 67).

participants.exclusions: Sample restricted to English petitions with fewer than 5,000 characters and at least 5 words and 2 sentences. Removed 15 of 432 sampled petitions for offensive language or personal identifying information, leaving 417 petitions (203 pre-AI, 214 post-AI). These exclusions count outputs; unique writers are not reported (PDF p. 67).
participants.who: Random sample of 432 English petitions (216 pre-AI, 216 post-AI); 15 removed for offensive language or personal information, leaving 417 (203 pre-AI, 214 post-AI). Rated by 14 Cornell Tech graduate students, each rating 80-90 petitions, three ratings per petition.
participants.country: Not stated for the sample; petitions drawn from the study dataset
participants.quote: This left us with a sample of 417 petitions (203 pre-AI, 214 post-AI).
participants.locator: p. 67, SI Petition Writing Quality and Persuasiveness

ai_tool.name_model: Change.org in-platform 'write with AI' tool built on an OpenAI-provided LLM
ai_tool.how_used: Post-AI petitions were written with access to the drafting tool; the authors' classifier flags 9.4% of pre-AI and 53.3% of post-AI sampled petitions as AI-written (SI Fig. 3, p. 25)

task.description: Writing real advocacy petitions on Change.org; raters scored them on 1-5 Likert items for writing quality and persuasiveness (SI Table 4)

outcomes.name: Writing quality score (mean of Likert items adapted from Noy and Zhang)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average of four writing-quality items covering structure, logical organization, clarity, and freedom from grammar, punctuation and spelling errors. Each item uses a 1-5 Likert scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree), adapted from Noy and Zhang. Three ratings per petition; the analysis compares petition scores using a two-sided Welch t-test (PDF p. 59, SI Table 4; p. 67, SI labeling task). The reported confidence interval accompanies Cohen's d; no mean-difference SE or arm SDs are supplied.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-AI petitions (written with in-platform AI access), n = 214
contrasts.reported: Pre-AI mean 2.73, post-AI mean 3.43; Welch t-test mu_post-pre = 0.70, t(412.46) = 9.76, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.96, Cohen's d 95% CI = [0.75, 1.16]
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Petition Text Quality; p. 67, SI Petition Writing Quality and Persuasiveness; p. 26, SI Figure 4a

outcomes.name: Persuasiveness score (mean of four Likert items on believable and convincing reasons, changing reader behavior, and influencing decision-makers)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average of four persuasiveness items: believable reasons, convincing reasons, potential to change reader behavior, and potential to influence decision-makers. Each item uses a 1-5 Likert scale (strongly disagree to strongly agree). Three ratings per petition; two-sided Welch t-test of petition scores (PDF p. 59, SI Table 4; p. 67, SI labeling task). The reported confidence interval accompanies Cohen's d; no mean-difference SE or arm SDs are supplied.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Post-AI petitions (written with in-platform AI access), n = 214
contrasts.reported: Pre-AI mean 2.46, post-AI mean 3.12; Welch t-test mu_post-pre = 0.66, t(414.56) = 8.75, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 0.86, Cohen's d 95% CI = [0.65, 1.06]
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Petition Text Quality; p. 67, SI Petition Writing Quality and Persuasiveness; p. 26, SI Figure 4b

studies.label: Repeat petition writers (first vs second petition by AI-access cohort)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No assignment. Returning writers were grouped retrospectively by whether their first and second petitions were written before or after in-platform AI access: Pre/Pre, Pre/Post and Post/Post (PDF pp. 7-8).
assignment.quote: We conduct an exploratory descriptive analysis of repeat petition writers.
assignment.locator: PDF pp. 7-8, Repeat Petition Writers; pp. 74-75, SI Repeat Petition Writers. Within-writer petition order is compared across non-random cohorts.
assignment.prereg_locator: PDF p. 75 calls this analysis exploratory; p. 66 lists preregistrations for the main causal analysis and labeling task, but none specifically for repeat writers.

arms.name: Pre/Post cohort
arms.description: First petition without in-platform AI access; second petition with access. Count is analyzed writers (PDF p. 7, Figure 3).

arms.name: Pre/Pre cohort
arms.description: Both petitions without in-platform AI access. Count is analyzed writers (PDF p. 7, Figure 3).

arms.name: Post/Post cohort
arms.description: Both petitions with in-platform AI access. Count is analyzed writers (PDF p. 7, Figure 3).

participants.exclusions: Writers whose second petition was within 6 months of the first, petitions during the A/B test period, and the final month of 2024 are excluded (PDF p. 74). Table 21 specifies that 72 observations with negative Flesch-Kincaid grades are removed only from the log-FKGL model, leaving 9,150 observations there; MATTR, word-count and engagement models use 9,222 petitions (PDF pp. 63-64, SI Tables 20-21). Writer count for the reduced FKGL model is not stated.
participants.who: Change.org users in the US, Great Britain, and Canada who wrote two petitions between January 2022 and November 30, 2024: Pre/Pre cohort N = 1,145, Pre/Post N = 2,669, Post/Post N = 797 (9,222 petitions)
participants.quote: Returning petition writers (N=4,611 users) from treated countries, on average, write longer petitions with worse outcomes when their second petition is written with access to AI.
participants.locator: PDF p. 7, Figure 3 (4,611 writers and cohort sizes); p. 14, Repeat Petition Writers; pp. 63-64, SI Tables 20-21 (model-specific counts); pp. 74-75, SI Repeat Petition Writers

ai_tool.name_model: Change.org in-platform 'write with AI' tool built on an OpenAI-provided LLM
ai_tool.how_used: Access to the drafting tool for petitions written after the full launch

task.description: Writing real advocacy petitions on Change.org; outputs are scored for length (word count), within-petition lexical variation (MATTR), readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade), and comment/signature engagement (PDF pp. 7-8 and 14; pp. 63-64, SI Tables 20-21).

outcomes.name: Repeat-writer petition length: word count
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Petition-level word count; linear mixed model of natural log word count with cohort, petition order and their interaction, plus user random effects. Within-cohort first/second contrasts use Bonferroni adjustment (PDF pp. 8 and 14). Pre/Pre: ratio 1.061, z = 2.370, p = 0.0534, d = 0.072, ratio 95% CI [1.000, 1.127]; Post/Post: ratio 1.066, z = 2.140, p = 0.0950, d = 0.077, ratio 95% CI [0.993, 1.145] (p. 8). These comparisons are not randomized. Timing denotes AI availability during production, not an AI-removal follow-up.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Pre/Post cohort: second petition with AI access
contrasts.control_arm: Same Pre/Post writers: first petition without AI access
contrasts.reported: First-petition mean word count 213.70 (95% CI [202.44, 227.68]); second-petition mean 250.27 (95% CI [241.49, 259.20]). Bonferroni-adjusted model contrast: second petitions 39% longer; ratio = 1.394, z = 20.353, p < .0001, Cohen's d = 0.399, ratio 95% CI [1.340, 1.450]. Model uses 9,222 petitions.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8, Repeat Petition Writers; p. 14, model specification; p. 64, SI Table 21

contrasts.reported: Log-word-count model interaction, Second Petition x Cohort (Pre/Post): coefficient 0.273, SE 0.030, *** (p < 0.001); Num.Obs. 9222. This is the additional change relative to Pre/Pre, not the within-Pre/Post ratio.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 64, SI Table 21; p. 75, SI Repeat Petition Writers

outcomes.name: Repeat-writer petition outcome: at least one comment within 30 days
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Binary petition-level engagement endpoint, excluding author comments; logistic mixed model with cohort, petition order, their interaction and user random effects. Within-cohort contrasts are Bonferroni adjusted (PDF pp. 8, 12 and 14). Pre/Pre: OR = 0.825, z = -1.911, p = 0.168, 95% CI [0.648, 1.050]; Post/Post: OR = 0.662, z = -3.382, p = 0.0022, 95% CI [0.495, 0.887] (p. 8). The Pre/Post-by-second-petition interaction has no significance marker in Table 20 (p. 63); the within-cohort contrast below is not a randomized effect or a DiD estimate. The unsuccessful-first-petition subgroup also showed no evidence of improved second-petition outcomes with AI (p. 8). The primary endpoint from S1 is reused in this exploratory analysis; a separate S3 preregistration is not stated.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Pre/Post cohort: second petition with AI access
contrasts.control_arm: Same Pre/Post writers: first petition without AI access
contrasts.reported: First petitions: 40.50% (95% CI [38.67, 42.38]); second petitions: 35.71% (95% CI [33.87, 37.32]). Bonferroni-adjusted logistic-model contrast: OR = 0.754, z = -4.236, p = 0.0001, 95% CI [0.642, 0.884]. Model uses 9,222 petitions.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 8, Repeat Petition Writers; p. 63, SI Table 20

outcomes.name: Repeat-writer within-petition lexical diversity: MATTR
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: MATTR over title and body, computed with 50-word windows (PDF pp. 11-12). Linear mixed model of untransformed MATTR with cohort, petition order, their interaction and user random effects (pp. 14 and 75). This is vocabulary variation within each petition, not inter-writer diversity. Supplementary Figure 33 presents descriptive first/second petition values with bootstrapped intervals (p. 52).

contrasts.reported: MATTR model interaction, Second Petition x Cohort (Pre/Post): coefficient 0.031, SE 0.002, *** (p < 0.001); Num.Obs. 9222. This is an interaction relative to the Pre/Pre cohort, not a raw second-minus-first difference within Pre/Post.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 64, SI Table 21; p. 75, SI Repeat Petition Writers

outcomes.name: Repeat-writer text complexity: Flesch-Kincaid grade level
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Linear mixed model of log-transformed Flesch-Kincaid grade level with cohort, petition order, their interaction and user random effects (PDF pp. 14 and 75). Higher grade levels mean more complex text. Table 21 removes 72 observations with negative grades from this model only, leaving 9,150 petition observations; the number of distinct writers remaining is not stated (p. 64).

contrasts.reported: Log-Flesch-Kincaid model interaction, Second Petition x Cohort (Pre/Post): coefficient 0.176, SE 0.017, *** (p < 0.001); Num.Obs. 9150. This is an interaction relative to Pre/Pre on the log scale; no transformed effect has been calculated.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 64, SI Table 21; p. 75, SI Repeat Petition Writers

outcomes.name: Repeat-writer petition outcome: at least ten signatures
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Binary petition-level indicator for at least 10 signatures at collection, not a timed signature endpoint (PDF p. 12). Logistic mixed model with cohort, petition order, their interaction and user random effects (pp. 14 and 75). Figure 33 and the SI describe lower second-petition engagement in Pre/Post writers (pp. 52 and 75); the reported interaction below compares their change against Pre/Pre writers and has no significance marker.

contrasts.reported: 10+ signatures logistic-model interaction, Second Petition x Cohort (Pre/Post): coefficient -0.033, SE 0.120; no significance marker. Num.Obs. 9222. Coefficient is on the log-odds scale; an exact p-value and CI for this term are not printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 63, SI Table 20; p. 75, SI Repeat Petition Writers

company_involvement.description: No formal data-sharing collaboration with Change.org (PDF p. 65). The authors confirmed country launch dates with Change.org staff, including personal communications with two employees about the Australian delay (pp. 2 and 65). The paper reports no specific funding for this work and no competing interests; it acknowledges Cornell fellowship support for the first author (p. 15). The false flag denotes no formal company collaboration or disclosed company funding; informal staff communications are recorded here.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 2, Results; p. 65, SI Change.org and the Write with AI Tool; p. 15, Acknowledgments and Competing Interests

eligibility.reason: No study randomly assigns people to AI. Access varies by country and time; the authors say the delay was not an intentional experiment "as far as the authors are aware" (PDF p. 65). The platform A/B test is excluded from the main DiD because individual access is unknown (p. 3); random petition sampling or assignment to raters in S2 is not random assignment of writers to AI (p. 67). Criterion 2 is met by S3, which analyzes 4,611 writers (p. 7, Figure 3); S1 and S2 report petitions, not distinct writer counts. Criterion 3 is met by homogeneity computed on petition outputs (p. 5), output quality ratings (p. 67), and output length in S3 (pp. 7-8). No study meets all three criteria. This is observational context, including a non-random within-writer analysis, not a core experiment.

one_line_finding: On Change.org, non-random in-platform AI access increased petition similarity by 0.056 (95% CI [0.049, 0.063]; PDF p. 5 and p. 61, SI Table 14) and post-AI petitions had higher rated writing quality (2.73 to 3.43, d = 0.96; p. 67), while engagement did not improve: the main month-clustered signature estimate was -5.33 percentage points (p = .001; p. 6), became non-significant with country clustering (p = 0.074; p. 61, SI Table 16), and the comment estimate was -2.51 points (p = 0.187; p. 6).
notes: All locators refer to PDF page numbers, including SI pages. The entire markdown conversion, including appendices, was read; recorded numerical results were checked against PDF text and tables. AI availability refers to the in-platform drafting tool, not verified individual use; off-platform AI could occur in comparison groups (PDF p. 3). MATTR measures vocabulary variation within a petition and is coded other, not across-people diversity. Additional sentence-count and readability measures are recorded as lexical robustness variants rather than separate outcomes (pp. 34 and 69). Descriptive sentiment, title-concreteness, individual verb-frequency, English-variety and topic-composition analyses are not extracted as separate creativity effects; they describe stylistic or compositional properties rather than rated creativity or a direct inter-writer diversity metric (SI pp. 68-74). Platform participation and production counts concern participation rather than output-scored creative performance (pp. 7 and 76). S3 is exploratory and non-random; its within-cohort ratios and its between-cohort interaction coefficients are labeled separately. Printed table p-values of 0.000 are retained as printed, without treating them as exact zero. Data/code URLs identify the author-provided source and were not independently downloaded.
